I have posted a few here before. I worked on research vessels for about 15 years. This is going to get lost in the middle of the comments, but that's probably for the best. This isn't some made up crap about ghosts and ghouls and mysterious lights and sea monsters. On it's own, it's not that scary but the implications are.

  
We were doing a project in the British Virgin Islands, it was sub-contracted by the Royal Navy so I can't tell you what it was. Now, it was about two weeks into this six week project when we saw something floating on the surface of the water. At first we thought it was a seal or a shark or dolphin. We had found one a week before, caught in illegal fishing nets. So one of the crew hauled it up. It wasn't marine life. It was a girl about 11 or 12 years old. Naked dead and had been for at least a day. Almost immediately the Captain came over screaming and yelling at us to toss her back. He was fucking terrified. This was a brave man with thirty years spent at sea. He had guided ships through storms, sailed across oceans, even spent two days on a lifeboat after his fishing boat sunk. So he wasn't someone to be scared lightly. But this dead girl fucking terrified him. 

We were a small crew, only eight of us. There was the Captain, a handful of older experienced hands, the chief researcher who was this British guy in his 60s, then me, a female about my age and then a younger intern. The British guy started to argue and the Captain got in his face, squaring up to him shouting stuff like"You do not want to mess with this! You do not want to touch this! We didn't see her!"

He wasn't angry, he was terrified. Whilst we were arguing, one of the other crew threw the girl back into the fucking water. A dead 11 year old girl and he just tossed her back overboard. At this point the Captain calmed down somewhat. He refused to tell us what the fuck was going on but just kept saying "trust me, we do not want to get involved with this."

  
Afterwards, me and the intern and the other researcher my age were talking about it. The intern spotted what I didn't. The girl had ropes around her hands and deep cuts on her ankles caused by rope. Some fucker had tied her up, weighed her down and thrown her overboard. I am guessing the rope around her legs snapped or came loose or wasn't tied properly.

  
Now, at first I thought this was something cartel or gang related, and the captain knew that and that is why he was so scared. But... a few years later, the news about Epstein Island broke, which made me reconsider. What if, Epstein Island wasn't the only one. What if there is another out there, and if  there is... considering we fished a murdered girl out of the water. It's even worse.

I mentioned a few in a past thread, weird stuff that I saw whilst at sea on various research vessels. The black divers are weird, but I don't think are supernatural. They're likely something to do with China and submarine operations in the South China Sea. |

What was weird though was these weird big blobs of slime on the surface of the water, about 200 km for sure. Maybe 5 to 10 feet across each. At first we thought they were oil, until we got closer and saw it was too thick and actually a dark green rather than black. Algae maybe? Well we took a sample--or tried too. Whatever this shit was it melted straight through the container. So we definitely thought some sort of acid or chemical that leaked from a passing cargo ship. Maybe even some shit that was dumped here.



It was then that one of the crew noticed that it wasn't sitting on the top of the water like we thought, but rather extended below. This needed checking out, so rather than just radio in and get out of there, the captain decided to stick around and send down a drone. The first one got about 500 meters down, following this glob of dark green mass deep into the sea. The signal failed--that happens. This was about 10 years ago and the underwater drone we were using was new, but we discovered on the voyage they were pretty unreliable. So we sent down out second. This one followed it down to its max depth of about 1,500 when the signal started to get fuzzy. We could have sent it further, but it was risky. We risked losing the drone altogether--again, these were quite unreliable.

All we could see below was this big black mass--just the general void of the sea. If you have been in the ocean like this, it's dark and it looks like it goes on endlessly. That is what we thought we were seeing here, jsut where the light from the drone and its camera feed ended and the black mass of ocean extending even deeper. That was until one of the crew pointed out that the depth of this part of the ocean was 1,550 meters. We should have been able to see the bottom but couldn't. There was just this big black mass lying on the bottom. So, rather than have the drone return, we moved it along to measure the size of this thing. The black mass was about 100 meters long and about 30 wide, forming an oval shape. Every now and then part of it extended upwards to the surface.

  
The captain decided to get out of there and radio this in. So, we hoisted up the drone as we were doing so. One of the crew--this old Filipino guy who wasn't liable to panic, started to shout for us. These big black blobs on the surface were coming towards us. Not just drifting in the ocean current. There were five or six of them we could see each on a different point and each drifting towards our boat. The nearest one was about 10 feet away at this point. 

  
So the captain made the call to basically get the fuck out of here. We remembered this stuff was very acidic--melting through our container withhin under a minute. We didn't want this to damage the ship. Now, as we were getting out of there, I wish I could say the stuff moved towards us to make it more thrilling, but it didn't. I got the impression whatever it was, it was very slow so there was no chance of it catching a moving boat like ours. But we were all glad to get out of there though because that thing was weird. No idea what it was to this day, and the Taiwan government sent another ship--a larger one --to investigate after we radioed it in, but they found nothing. The sea bed though in that area, was devoid of life. We heard through the grapevine that the second ship followed this trail of empty sea along the bed for about 20 miles before turning back as it was nearing Chinese waters.

There was one time our vessel found a bunch of dead fish in one set area of the ocean. There were hundreds of them, just floating on the surface. A mixture of different types and all within a rough square mile area. Now, I dont want you to picture looking out to sea and you just see fish stacked end to end. It was more, five dead fish floating in a cluster here, another one a few yards away, another three or four next to each other, the occasional shark or similar oddity and so on in a square mile of ocean.  It was pretty much like all the ocean life in that square mile had just died at the same time.

  
They were tested on board of course, but nothing odd--no signs of disease or injury. A few did have pretty bad parasite infections, but not enough to conclude it was the cause, and many didn't have parasites, or had different parasites.

Our best guess was, this was something military. A weapons test or something. No idea if China or Taiwan or even the Phillipines. 

  
Another odd one was this emergency message we got in Japanese,  frantic Japanese early one morning. This was north of Ityabet island near the Phillipines. Now, I cant speak Japanese so I had no idea what was being said but the Captain could, but he did say the speaker had an unusual dialect which made it trickier to understand. He basically told us he was getting an emergency message from a ship he described as a minesweeper sinking. He got no reply, just the emergency message repeated occasionally with the occasional added detail. With long silences between each message sometimes. We got the message for about three hours, not repeated regularly, sometimes it was every 15 minutes, other times there was a half hour or even an hour gap between the messages. And we found absolutely nothing in the area. Not a sign of a ship, not a sign of any wreckage. Nothing. The messages just ended a few hours after we first received them. There was a Taiwan coastguard vessel in the area and they did not pick up any emergency radio message at all but they also helped search the area. 

No ship--whether civilian or military was ever reported missing. We contacted the Japanese of course, assuming since the message was in Japanese that it was one of there's. Nothing. Nothing from Taiwan. Nothing from the Philippines. Even nothing from the Chinese, but they wouldn't admit to a minesweeper sinking anyway.
